introduction-the-all-systems-green-falla.core: Dashboards can be all green (CPU fine, error rate low, latency OK) while the business is failing: checkouts dropped 40% because a payment provider silently declines cards, or a marketing link points to a 404. Technical health is necessary but not sufficient. Business observability monitors outcomes such as orders, sign-ups and revenue per minute alongside system signals.

first_principles.problem: An e-commerce site's orders fall by half for three hours while every technical alert stays quiet.
truths: Business outcomes are measurable in near real time.

analogy.title: A shop with working tills but no customers
analogy.story: The tills, lights and doors all function, yet nobody's buying because the sign outside says 'closed'.
analogy.breaks: Shopkeepers see empty floors; services need explicit KPI metrics.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Orders per minute visible beside error rates.

code.text:
ORDERS = Counter("orders_completed_total", "Completed orders", ["country", "payment_method"])
REVENUE = Counter("order_revenue_cents_total", "Revenue", ["country", "currency"])
def on_order_completed(order):
    ORDERS.labels(order.country, order.payment_method).inc()
    REVENUE.labels(order.country, order.currency).inc(order.total_cents)

check.q: Why can technical metrics be green during a business outage?
check.a: Systems may respond successfully while producing bad outcomes (declined payments, broken flows), which only business metrics reveal.

mapping-technical-metrics-to-business-kp.core: Connect each business KPI to the user journey and services behind it: checkout conversion depends on cart, pricing, payment and fraud services, and their latency and errors. Mapping lets you translate technical degradation into business impact ('p99 +500 ms on payment correlates with −3% conversion') and prioritise work by business value. Use journey funnels and shared dimensions (country, platform) on both sides.

first_principles.problem: Engineering can't explain why a 300 ms latency regression matters, so the fix is deprioritised.

analogy.title: A factory's output traced to each machine
analogy.story: If widgets per hour drop, you know which machines on the line could be responsible.
analogy.breaks: Factory lines are linear; user journeys branch.

check.q: Why use the same dimensions (e.g. country, platform) for business and technical metrics?
check.a: So you can correlate KPI changes with technical signals for the same segment of users.

revenue-at-risk-quantifying-downtime.core: Revenue at risk converts incidents into money. Expected revenue per minute (from historical baselines for that time and day) multiplied by the fraction of affected traffic and the duration gives approximate lost or at-risk revenue. It turns SLO and incident discussions into business language, justifies reliability investment, and helps decide incident severity in real time.

first_principles.problem: Leadership asks 'how bad was the outage?' and engineering can only answer in error percentages.
truths: Impact scales with affected share and time.

analogy.title: A shop calculating losses from a closed hour
analogy.story: If Saturdays at noon usually bring $5,000 per hour, a one-hour closure risks about $5,000.
analogy.breaks: Shops lose walk-ins; online users often retry later.

check.q: Why use a time-of-week baseline instead of a daily average for revenue at risk?
check.a: Traffic and revenue vary strongly by hour and weekday, so a matching baseline gives a far more accurate estimate.

anomaly-detection-handling-seasonality.core: Business metrics have strong seasonality (daily, weekly, holidays), so static thresholds fail: 100 orders per minute is great at 3 a.m. and terrible at noon. Anomaly detection compares against expected values: same time last week (offset 1w), rolling seasonal baselines, or models like Holt-Winters and Prophet, with alerts when the deviation (ratio or z-score) persists. Account for known events such as sales and holidays.

first_principles.problem: A static 'orders < 200/min' alert fires every night and misses a 40% drop during the lunch peak.
derivation: Compare to **same time last week** (or several weeks).

analogy.title: Comparing this Monday's footfall to last Monday's
analogy.story: Low on Sunday night is normal; low on Monday lunchtime is alarming.
analogy.breaks: Shops know holidays; models must be told.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Catches lunch-peak drops, quiet at night.

check.q: Why average several weeks of offset data for a baseline?
check.a: A single prior week might itself contain an anomaly or event; averaging several weeks gives a more robust expected value.

the-business-observability-dashboard.core: A business observability dashboard shows outcomes first: KPIs (orders per minute, conversion, revenue, sign-ups) with seasonal baselines, then journey funnels, then supporting SLIs (latency and errors of key services), with deploy and incident annotations and breakdowns by country, platform and payment method. It's a shared view for product, business and engineering during incidents and launches.

first_principles.problem: During a launch, product, marketing and engineering each watch different dashboards and miss the connection between a slow API and falling conversions.

analogy.title: A cockpit primary flight display
analogy.story: Altitude, speed and heading front and centre, with engine details below for diagnosis.
analogy.breaks: Cockpits are standardised; dashboards must be designed per business.
